summary: After two more years of Joseph's imprisonment, Pharaoh's paired dreams lead the cup bearer to remember him, and Joseph interprets seven years of abundance followed by seven of famine. Pharaoh appoints him to oversee a grain reserve; Joseph establishes a household, stores vast harvests, and sells grain when famine brings Egypt and other lands to him.
whyItMatters: Joseph's reversal from prisoner to administrator creates the means by which his family will survive. The chapter joins credited divine insight to practical planning while establishing the concentrated authority through which food will be distributed.

context.author: Genesis names no narrator or final compiler. Tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the history of its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel reflecting on its ancestral promises, family relationships, and arrival in Egypt. The chapter does not identify a more specific original audience.
context.date: The ancestral story is set earlier than the book’s final literary form. Its composition and editing developed over time, with exact dates and models debated.
context.setting: Pharaoh's court and the cities and fields of Egypt across seven years of abundance and the onset of famine.
context.literaryForm: Royal dream narrative, interpretation and policy proposal, investiture, birth notices, and fulfillment.

before.text: The cup bearer's restored position fulfilled Joseph's interpretation, but he forgot Joseph's plea for release. Pharaoh's dreams finally renew the connection after two full years.

here.text: The dreams are explained, a plan is proposed, and Joseph receives the authority to collect and sell the grain that will bring his brothers to Egypt.

after.text: Famine in Canaan sends ten of Joseph's brothers to buy food; they bow before him without recognizing the brother they sold.

outline.heading: Pharaoh’s dreams and the cup bearer’s memory
outline.note: No court interpreter resolves the dreams, and the officer recalls Joseph.

outline.heading: Joseph summoned and the dreams retold
outline.note: Joseph credits God, and Pharaoh describes the devouring cattle and grain.

outline.heading: Interpretation and a storage proposal
outline.note: Seven years of plenty and seven of famine call for organized reserves.

outline.heading: Appointment over Egypt
outline.note: Pharaoh grants authority, public honors, a new name, and a wife.

outline.heading: Abundant storage and two sons
outline.note: Joseph stores grain and interprets his sons’ names through his experience.

outline.heading: Famine and grain sales
outline.note: The promised famine arrives, and buyers from many lands come to Joseph.

keyVerses.text: Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, “It isn’t in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”
keyVerses.why: Joseph attributes the answer to God when Pharaoh credits him with interpretive skill.

keyVerses.text: The food will be to supply the land against the seven years of famine, which will be in the land of Egypt; so that the land will not perish through the famine.”
keyVerses.why: The storage plan has an explicitly life-preserving purpose.

keyVerses.text: The famine was over all the surface of the earth. Joseph opened all the store houses, and sold to the Egyptians. The famine was severe in the land of Egypt.
keyVerses.why: The reserve becomes grain sold under Joseph’s authority during severe famine.

questions.question: Why are the two dreams interpreted as one?
questions.answer: Both sets of seven represent the same sequence of abundant years followed by famine. Joseph says the repetition signifies that God has established the matter and will bring it about soon.

questions.question: What does Joseph propose beyond interpreting the dreams?
questions.answer: He recommends a wise administrator, local overseers, collection of a fifth of the produce during plenty, and storage in cities. Interpretation becomes a concrete plan intended to prevent the land from perishing.

questions.question: Is Joseph’s authority unlimited?
questions.answer: Pharaoh places him over the household and land, gives public signs of office, and requires obedience to his word. Pharaoh nevertheless explicitly retains superiority in the throne, so Joseph's extraordinary power is delegated royal power.

questions.question: What is the function of Pharaoh’s “signet ring”?
questions.answer: It is one of the objects transferred to Joseph when he receives office, alongside fine clothing and a gold chain. In the scene it visibly marks Pharaoh's authorization; the chapter does not explain particular administrative documents or procedures.

questions.question: Do Joseph’s new names erase his earlier suffering?
questions.answer: His naming speeches say God has made him forget toil and made him fruitful, yet he still calls Egypt the land of his affliction. The paired statements describe relief and new life without requiring that all pain or attachment to his father's house has vanished.

questions.question: Is the stored grain simply handed out free?
questions.answer: The chapter says Joseph opens the storehouses and sells to Egyptians, and that other countries come to buy. It establishes access through a state-controlled reserve but does not yet describe all the later costs or terms of the famine economy.

questions.question: Does successful interpretation tell readers how to decode any dream?
questions.answer: This story gives Joseph a specific explanation of Pharaoh's paired dreams and narrates its fulfillment. It does not offer a universal symbolic dictionary in which cattle or grain always mean the same thing.

glossary.def: The share of Egypt’s produce Joseph proposes collecting during the abundant years.
Pharaoh’s ring transferred to Joseph as a sign of entrusted authority.
The grain reserves Joseph opens for sales when the famine becomes severe.
